complexityReason: We binary search only the smaller array, which is O(log min(m, n)); simplified as O(log n). Only boundary variables and pointers are stored, so space is O(1).

title: Reverse Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.

patternReason.right: Linked list fits because the task is about rewiring each node's next pointer in place.

wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is needed; the problem is pointer manipulation.
wrong.Two pointers: Two variables are used, but this is not the opposite-end two-pointer pattern.
wrong.Stack: A stack can reverse order, but it uses extra memory and misses the in-place pointer idea.
wrong.Binary search: The list is not sorted for search and random access is unavailable.
wrong.Dynamic programming: There are no overlapping subproblems.

approach.content:
Reverse the direction of every next pointer.

  1. Keep prev as the reversed part and cur as the current node.
  2. Save cur.next before changing it.
  3. Point cur.next to prev, then move both pointers forward.
  4. When cur becomes null, prev is the new head.

complexityReason: Each node is visited once, so time is O(n). Only a few pointers are stored, so space is O(1).

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problem: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted list and return its head.

patternReason.right: Linked list fits because we build the answer by relinking nodes from two linked lists.

wrong.Hash map: No value lookup is needed.
wrong.Two pointers: There are two cursors, but the core operation is linked-list merging and pointer attachment.
wrong.Binary search: Linked lists do not support efficient random access.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No repeated subproblem state is being reused.

approach.content:
Use a dummy node to avoid special handling for the first merged node.

  1. Compare the current nodes of both lists.
  2. Attach the smaller node to the merged tail.
  3. Advance the list that contributed the node.
  4. Attach the remaining non-empty list at the end.

complexityReason: Each node from both lists is attached once, so time is O(n + m). The merge reuses existing nodes and only stores dummy/tail pointers, so space is O(1).

title: Reorder List
problem: Given the head of a linked list, reorder it as L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 and so on. Modify the list in-place.

patternReason.right: Fast/slow pointers fit because the first key step is finding the middle of the linked list without knowing its length upfront.

wrong.Hash map: Index lookup is not necessary and would use extra memory.
wrong.Sorting: The list order is structural, not sorted by value.
wrong.Binary search: No sorted searchable range exists.
wrong.Sliding window: There is no contiguous window condition.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.

approach.content:
Split, reverse, then weave.

  1. Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle.
  2. Reverse the second half.
  3. Merge the first half and reversed second half by alternating nodes.
  4. Do everything by changing next pointers.

complexityReason: Finding the middle, reversing, and merging are each linear passes, so total time is O(n). Only pointers are used, so space is O(1).

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problem: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return its head.

patternReason.right: Fast/slow pointers fit because keeping a fixed gap of n nodes lets one pointer identify the node before the target in one pass.

wrong.Hash map: Storing node positions works but is unnecessary extra memory.
wrong.Sorting: Node order must not be sorted.
wrong.Binary search: Linked lists do not support random access.
wrong.Sliding window: This is a pointer gap, not a variable-size subarray window.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No reusable subproblem structure exists.

approach.content:
Create a gap of n nodes between two pointers.

  1. Use a dummy before head to handle deleting the first node.
  2. Move fast ahead by n steps.
  3. Move fast and slow together until fast.next is null.
  4. slow.next is the node to delete.

complexityReason: The list is traversed with two pointers in one linear pass after the initial gap, so time is O(n). Only a dummy and pointers are stored, so space is O(1).

title: Copy List With Random Pointer
problem: Given a linked list where each node has next and random pointers, return a deep copy of the list.
example:
head = [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]
output = deep copied list with the same next/random structure

patternReason.right: Hash map fits because each original node must map to exactly one copied node so random pointers can be rebuilt correctly.

wrong.Linked list: The structure is a linked list, but the key trick is mapping originals to copies.
wrong.Two pointers: No opposite-end or gap pointer strategy solves random references.
wrong.Binary search: There is no sorted search space.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.

approach.content:
Build a mapping from old nodes to new nodes.

  1. First pass: create a copy node for every original node.
  2. Second pass: assign each copy's next and random using the map.
  3. Return the copied version of head.

complexityReason: Two passes over n nodes make time O(n). The map stores one copied node per original node, so space is O(n).

title: Add Two Numbers
problem: Given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers in reverse digit order, add them and return the sum as a linked list.

patternReason.right: Linked list fits because the sum is built digit by digit while traversing linked-list nodes and maintaining carry.

wrong.Hash map: No key-based lookup is needed.
wrong.Two pointers: There are two list cursors, but the core pattern is linked-list digit construction with carry.
wrong.Stack: Digits are already reversed, so stack reversal is unnecessary.
wrong.Binary search: No sorted search space exists.
wrong.Dynamic programming: There is no overlapping subproblem recurrence.

approach.content:
Simulate elementary addition from least significant digit to most significant digit.

  1. Use a dummy head for the result.
  2. Add current digits plus carry.
  3. Create a node with sum % 10.
  4. Carry becomes sum // 10.
  5. Continue while either list or carry remains.

optimalCode: while l1 or l2 or carry:
l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
complexityReason: Each input node is processed once, so time is O(n + m). Ignoring the returned output list, only carry and pointers are stored, so auxiliary space is O(1).

title: Linked List Cycle
problem: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle.

patternReason.right: Fast/slow pointers fit because if a cycle exists, a faster pointer will eventually lap and meet the slower pointer.

wrong.Hash map: A visited set works, but fast/slow detects the cycle with constant space.
wrong.Sorting: Node order is not sortable for cycle detection.
wrong.Binary search: There is no sorted range.
wrong.Sliding window: No window is being maintained.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.

approach.content:
Use Floyd's cycle detection.

  1. Move slow one step and fast two steps.
  2. If they ever point to the same node, there is a cycle.
  3. If fast reaches null, the list ends and has no cycle.

complexityReason: Fast and slow pointers visit at most a linear number of nodes before meeting or reaching the end, so time is O(n). Only two pointers are used, so space is O(1).

title: Find the Duplicate Number
problem: Given an array nums containing n + 1 integers where each integer is in [1, n], return the repeated number without modifying the array and using constant extra space.

patternReason.right: Fast/slow pointers fit because values can be treated as next pointers, turning the array into a functional graph with a cycle.

wrong.Hash map: A set finds duplicates but uses O(n) extra space.
wrong.Sorting: Sorting modifies the array or requires extra memory.
wrong.Binary search: Value-range binary search is possible, but the classic constant-space approach is cycle detection.
wrong.Sliding window: No contiguous subarray window is involved.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No recurrence or overlapping subproblem exists.

approach.content:
Treat each index as a node and nums[i] as the next pointer.

  1. Use Floyd's algorithm to find an intersection inside the cycle.
  2. Reset one pointer to the start.
  3. Move both one step at a time.
  4. The node where they meet is the duplicate value.

complexityReason: Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time over the implicit graph. It stores only a few indices, so space is O(1).

title: LRU Cache
problem: Design a data structure that supports get and put in O(1) average time and evicts the least recently used key when capacity is exceeded.
example:
LRUCache cache = LRUCache(2)
put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3)
key 2 is evicted

patternReason.right: Hash map fits because O(1) key lookup is required; it is paired with a doubly linked list to track recency.

wrong.Linked list: A linked list tracks recency, but alone it cannot find keys in O(1).
wrong.Heap: A heap gives priority removal but updating recency on every access is not clean O(1).
wrong.Queue: A queue cannot remove arbitrary recently accessed keys in O(1).
wrong.Binary search: Ordering by key does not solve least-recently-used eviction.
wrong.Dynamic programming: This is a data structure design problem, not a recurrence.

approach.content:
Combine two structures.

  1. Hash map: key → linked-list node for O(1) lookup.
  2. Doubly linked list: most recent near the front, least recent near the back.
  3. On every get/put, move the node to the front.
  4. When capacity is exceeded, remove the tail node.

bruteCode: self.items = [(k, v) for k, v in self.items if k != key]
complexityReason: Each get/put does constant-time hash map and doubly linked-list operations on average. The cache stores up to capacity nodes, so space is O(n).

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problem: Given an array of k linked-list heads, merge all lists into one sorted linked list and return it.

patternReason.right: Heap fits because we repeatedly need the smallest current head among k sorted lists.

wrong.Linked list: The input is linked lists, but the key operation is repeatedly choosing the minimum among k candidates.
wrong.Hash map: Lookup does not help maintain the next smallest node.
wrong.Binary search: There is no single sorted array to search.
wrong.Sliding window: No window condition exists.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems are reused.

approach.content:
Keep the current smallest candidate from each list in a min-heap.

  1. Push each non-empty list head into the heap.
  2. Pop the smallest node and attach it to the result.
  3. If that node has a next node, push the next node.
  4. Repeat until the heap is empty.

complexityReason: There are n total nodes. Each node is pushed/popped from a heap of size at most k, so time is O(n log k). The heap stores at most k nodes, so space is O(k).

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
problem: Given a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time and return the modified list. Nodes left over with fewer than k should remain unchanged.

patternReason.right: Linked list fits because the solution repeatedly rewires next pointers within fixed-size groups.

wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is needed.
wrong.Two pointers: Pointers are used, but the main task is group-wise linked-list reversal.
wrong.Stack: A stack can reverse groups but uses extra memory.
wrong.Binary search: No sorted search space exists.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.

approach.content:
Reverse one confirmed group at a time.

  1. Use a helper to find the kth node from the current group start.
  2. If fewer than k nodes remain, stop.
  3. Reverse pointers inside that group.
  4. Reconnect the previous group to the newly reversed group.

complexityReason: Every node is reversed at most once, so time is O(n). The optimal version uses only pointers, so auxiliary space is O(1).

title: Invert Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree and return its root.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because each node is visited recursively and its left/right children are swapped.

wrong.Binary search: The task is not searching a sorted structure.
wrong.Sliding window: There is no contiguous window.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is needed.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is involved.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems are reused.

approach.content:
At every node, swap its children.

  1. If the node is null, return null.
  2. Swap left and right.
  3. Recursively invert both subtrees.
  4. Return the root.

complexityReason: Every node is visited once, so time is O(n). Recursive call stack depth is the tree height h, so space is O(h).

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because the depth of a node is computed from the depths of its left and right subtrees.

wrong.Binary search: No sorted search is happening.
wrong.Sliding window: No contiguous window exists.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is needed.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue behavior is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: This is recursive tree aggregation, not overlapping-state DP.

approach.content:
Ask each subtree for its height.

  1. An empty tree has depth 0.
  2. The depth of a node is 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth).
  3. Return that value up the recursion stack.

complexityReason: Each node contributes once to the depth calculation, so time is O(n). The recursion stack is O(h), where h is the height of the tree.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter, the number of edges in the longest path between any two nodes.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because each node needs subtree heights, and those heights also determine the best diameter through that node.

wrong.Binary search: No sorted search space exists.
wrong.Sliding window: No contiguous window exists.
wrong.Hash map: Lookup is not the core operation.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: Although it returns information upward, this is standard tree DFS without overlapping subproblems.

approach.content:
Compute height and update the best diameter during the same DFS.

  1. For each node, get left height and right height.
  2. The path through that node has length left + right.
  3. Update the global best.
  4. Return 1 + max(left, right) as the node height.

complexityReason: The optimized DFS computes each subtree height once, so time is O(n). The recursion stack is O(h).

title: Balanced Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced, meaning the left and right subtree heights of every node differ by no more than 1.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because every node must report both its subtree height and whether that subtree is balanced.

wrong.Binary search: No ordered search is involved.
wrong.Sliding window: No window exists.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table solves the height condition.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: There are no overlapping states; the tree is traversed once.

approach.content:
Return height unless a subtree is already invalid.

  1. DFS into left and right children.
  2. If either side is unbalanced, bubble up failure.
  3. If heights differ by more than 1, mark failure.
  4. Otherwise return the current height.

complexityReason: Each node height is computed once in the optimized DFS, so time is O(n). The recursion stack takes O(h) space.

title: Same Tree
problem: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, determine if they are structurally identical and have the same node values.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because the decision depends on comparing the current pair of nodes, then recursively comparing left with left and right with right.

wrong.Binary tree BFS: BFS can work, but the cleanest pattern here is pairwise DFS over matching subtrees.
wrong.Binary search tree: The trees are not guaranteed to be BSTs.
wrong.Hash map: There is no lookup problem.
wrong.Dynamic programming: There are no overlapping subproblems.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is needed.

approach.content:
Compare both trees at the same position.

  1. If both nodes are null, that branch matches.
  2. If only one is null, the shape differs.
  3. If values differ, the trees differ.
  4. Otherwise compare left children and right children recursively.

bruteCode: if not p and not q:
if not p or not q:
return isSameTree(p.left, q.left) and isSameTree(p.right, q.right)
optimalCode: if not p and not q:
if not p or not q or p.val != q.val:
return isSameTree(p.left, q.left) and isSameTree(p.right, q.right)
complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(h). Each pair of matching nodes is visited once; recursion depth follows the tree height.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
problem: Given the roots of two binary trees root and subRoot, return true if subRoot is a subtree of root.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because we scan every node as a possible starting point, then use same-tree DFS to verify a match.

wrong.Binary tree BFS: BFS could find candidates, but subtree verification is naturally recursive.
wrong.Hash map: Hashing can optimize variants, but the standard solution is DFS.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No repeated state table is needed.
wrong.Heap: No min/max priority is involved.

approach.content:
Use two DFS functions.

  1. same(a,b) checks whether two trees are identical.
  2. Walk through root.
  3. At each node, test whether the subtree starting there equals subRoot.
  4. If not, search the left and right subtrees.

bruteCode: if not a and not b:
if not a or not b or a.val != b.val:
return same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)
return same(root, subRoot) or isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) or isSubtree(root.right, subRoot)
optimalCode: if not a and not b:
if not a or not b or a.val != b.val:
return same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)
return isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) or isSubtree(root.right, subRoot)
complexityReason: Time is O(n · m) and space is O(h). In the worst case, many nodes of the main tree may start a subtree comparison.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problem: Given a binary search tree and two nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor.

patternReason.right: Binary search tree fits because node values tell us whether both targets are left, both are right, or the current node splits them.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: A generic DFS works, but it ignores the BST ordering.
wrong.Binary tree BFS: Level traversal does not use sorted structure.
wrong.Hash map: Parent maps are unnecessary.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue is useful.

approach.content:
Use the BST property.

  1. If both targets are smaller than the current node, move left.
  2. If both are larger, move right.
  3. Otherwise the current node is where the paths split, so it is the LCA.

bruteCode: a, b = path(root, p), path(root, q)
for x, y in zip(a, b):
optimalCode: if p.val < cur.val and q.val < cur.val:
elif p.val > cur.val and q.val > cur.val:
complexityReason: Time is O(h) and space is O(1). The BST ordering lets us move down one path instead of scanning the full tree.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal from left to right, level by level.

patternReason.right: Binary tree BFS fits because the output is grouped by depth, and a queue naturally processes one level at a time.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: DFS can be adapted, but BFS directly matches level order.
wrong.Binary search tree: The tree is not necessarily ordered.
wrong.Hash map: No key lookup is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No repeated states exist.
wrong.Heap: We do not need priority ordering.

approach.content:
Process the tree level by level.

  1. Put the root in a queue.
  2. For each loop, capture the current queue size.
  3. Pop exactly that many nodes to form one level.
  4. Push their children for the next level.

complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(n). Every node is enqueued and dequeued once, and the queue can hold a full level.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values visible when viewing the tree from the right side.

patternReason.right: Binary tree BFS fits because the right side view is the last visible node at each depth.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: DFS can work with depth tracking, but level BFS makes the last node per level obvious.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is necessary.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping states exist.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is needed.

approach.content:
Use level order traversal.

  1. Traverse one level at a time.
  2. The last node popped from each level is the visible rightmost node.
  3. Add that value to the result.

complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(n). BFS visits every node once; the queue stores at most a level of the tree.

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
problem: Given a binary tree, count nodes that are good. A node is good if no value on the path from root to that node is greater than it.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because each recursive call only needs the maximum value seen on the path so far.

wrong.Binary tree BFS: BFS can carry the path max, but DFS is simpler and memory-light.
wrong.Hash map: No repeated lookup is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: There are no overlapping subproblems.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue is involved.

approach.content:
Carry path state during DFS.

  1. Start with max-so-far as negative infinity.
  2. A node is good if its value is at least that max.
  3. Update max-so-far before visiting children.
  4. Sum the counts from left and right.

optimalCode: return good + dfs(node.left, best) + dfs(node.right, best)
complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(h). DFS carries the maximum value seen so far and visits each node once.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree.

patternReason.right: Binary search tree fits because each node must fall within a valid lower and upper bound inherited from its ancestors.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: DFS is used, but the key idea is enforcing BST value ranges.
wrong.Binary tree BFS: Level order does not prove ordering constraints.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.
wrong.Heap: Heap ordering is different from BST ordering.

approach.content:
Do not only compare a node with its direct children.

  1. Every node has a valid range.
  2. Left children must be less than the current node and also respect ancestor bounds.
  3. Right children must be greater and respect ancestor bounds.
  4. If any node violates its range, return false.

bruteCode: return all(vals[i] < vals[i + 1] for i in range(len(vals) - 1))
optimalCode: return dfs(node.left, low, node.val) and dfs(node.right, node.val, high)
complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(h). Each node is checked once against a valid value range; recursion depth is tree height.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problem: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the kth smallest value in the tree.

patternReason.right: Binary search tree fits because an inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: DFS is used, but the critical insight is BST inorder ordering.
wrong.Binary tree BFS: BFS does not produce sorted order.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup by key is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No repeated states exist.
wrong.Heap: A heap could solve it, but it wastes the BST property.

approach.content:
Use inorder traversal.

  1. Visit left subtree first.
  2. Then visit the current node.
  3. Then visit right subtree.
  4. The kth visited value is the answer.

complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(h). In-order traversal may visit up to all nodes; the stack follows tree height.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
problem: Given preorder and inorder traversal arrays of a binary tree with unique values, build and return the original tree.

patternReason.right: Hash map fits because we need fast lookup of each root value inside the inorder array to split left and right subtrees.

wrong.Binary tree DFS: DFS builds the tree, but the key optimization is the inorder index map.
wrong.Binary tree BFS: The traversals describe recursive subtree boundaries, not level order.
wrong.Binary search tree: The tree is not necessarily a BST.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No overlapping subproblems exist.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is involved.

approach.content:
Preorder tells the next root. Inorder tells the size of the left and right subtrees.

  1. Map each inorder value to its index.
  2. Take the next preorder value as root.
  3. Use its inorder index to split left and right ranges.
  4. Recursively build left, then right.

bruteCode: if not preorder or not inorder:
optimalCode: idx = {val: i for i, val in enumerate(inorder)}
complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(n). The inorder index map gives O(1) split lookup for every node.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problem: Given a non-empty binary tree, return the maximum path sum. A path may start and end at any nodes, but it must follow parent-child links.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because each node must report the best one-sided path it can extend upward while updating a global best split path.

wrong.Binary tree BFS: Level order does not combine path gains correctly.
wrong.Hash map: No lookup table solves the path calculation.
wrong.Dynamic programming: Tree DP is related, but this is usually implemented as postorder DFS.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue is needed.

approach.content:
Separate two ideas.

  1. The path returned to the parent must be one-sided: node plus left or right.
  2. The answer at a node may split through both children.
  3. Ignore negative child gains because they reduce the sum.
  4. Update a global maximum at every node.

bruteCode: cur_paths += [node.val + x for x in left]
cur_paths += [node.val + x for x in right]
complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(h). Postorder DFS computes one-sided gains for each node once.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problem: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and deserialize the string back to the same tree.

patternReason.right: Binary tree DFS fits because preorder traversal with null markers captures both values and structure.

wrong.Binary tree BFS: BFS can also work, but preorder DFS with null markers is compact and direct.
wrong.Binary search tree: The tree is not necessarily a BST.
wrong.Hash map: No random lookup is required.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No repeated states exist.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is involved.

approach.content:
Values alone are not enough; null positions must also be saved.

  1. Serialize with preorder: node, left, right.
  2. Write a marker like N for null children.
  3. Deserialize by reading tokens in the same order.
  4. Each token either creates a node or returns null.

complexityReason: Time is O(n) and space is O(n). Both operations process every node/null marker once.

title: Implement Trie Prefix Tree
problem: Implement a prefix tree with insert, search, and startsWith operations.

patternReason.right: Trie fits because words share prefixes, and each operation walks one character at a time through prefix nodes.

wrong.Hash map: Hash maps are used inside trie nodes, but the overall structure is a trie.
wrong.Binary search: No sorted array search is needed.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No recurrence or overlapping states are involved.

approach.content:
A trie stores characters as edges.

  1. Each node has a children map.
  2. Insert walks/creates one node per character.
  3. Search walks characters and also checks an end-of-word flag.
  4. startsWith only checks whether the prefix path exists.

bruteCode: return any(w.startswith(prefix) for w in self.words)
complexityReason: Time is O(m) and space is O(n · m). Runtime depends on the length of the word or prefix, not the number of stored words.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
problem: Design a data structure that supports adding words and searching words where . can match any single character.

patternReason.right: Trie fits because normal characters follow prefix edges, while dot search branches across children at that trie node.

wrong.DFS backtracking: Search uses DFS inside the trie, but the data structure choice is the trie.
wrong.Hash map: Children maps help implement nodes, but a flat hash map cannot handle wildcard prefixes efficiently.
wrong.Binary search: The words are not searched as a sorted array.
wrong.Heap: No priority ordering is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: No memo table is necessary for the standard solution.

approach.content:
Use trie insertion, then DFS search for wildcards.

  1. Adding a word is the same as normal trie insert.
  2. During search, a normal letter moves to one child.
  3. A dot tries every child at that position.
  4. At the end, the current node must be marked as a word ending.

bruteCode: if all(a == b or b == '.' for a, b in zip(w, word)):
optimalCode: return any(dfs(i + 1, child) for child in node.children.values())
complexityReason: Time is O(26ᵐ) and space is O(n · m). Dots can branch to many children, so search can explore many trie nodes in the worst case.

title: Word Search II
problem: Given a board of characters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed by adjacent cells without reusing a cell in the same word.

patternReason.right: DFS backtracking fits because we explore board paths cell by cell; a trie is used with it to prune impossible prefixes early.

wrong.Trie: Trie is essential for pruning, but the action on the board is DFS backtracking.
wrong.Hash map: A hash set of words alone does not prune prefixes well.
wrong.Binary search: The board is not sorted.
wrong.Heap: No priority queue is needed.
wrong.Dynamic programming: Cells cannot be reused in a path, so simple DP states are not enough.

approach.content:
Combine trie prefix pruning with board DFS.

  1. Build a trie from all words.
  2. Start DFS from every board cell.
